hybridherbst

Last edited by hybridherbst

### Description
I think it would be useful to note somewhere which colors set throughout three are intended to be in linear or sRGB space.

As an example, the scene background ( [https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/scenes/Scene.background](https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/scenes/Scene.background)) just states it is a color, of course one can experiment if that is passed through as linear or sRGB to the shader. The same applies to e.g. material.color, light.color, and others. At least in the glTF spec there's differences between the color spaces (e.g. diffuse color is in sRGB, light color is in linear), but I'm not sure if in three everything is just sRGB and how that will/will not change once P3 and other wide gamut spaces are available.

ContributorAuthor

From looking at what the GLTFLoader does:

_material.color_

Line 668 in 24ccd56

|  |  |
|-|-|
|  | materialParams.color.setRGB(array[0],array[1],array[2],LinearSRGBColorSpace); |

is treated the same as

_light.color_

Line 550 in 24ccd56

|  |  |
|-|-|
|  | if(lightDef.color!==undefined)color.setRGB(lightDef.color[0],lightDef.color[1],lightDef.color[2],LinearSRGBColorSpace); |

~~despite the light being in linear space in glTF and the albedo color being in sRGB space in glTF.~~ ~~So I guess that means in three light.color and material.color are also using different color spaces.~~

In more recent versions of three.js we treat all THREE.Color instances alike, regardless of where they are used. Components (like `color.r`) are always in the working color space (currently "Linear-sRGB").

Certain setters — for hexadecimal and CSS strings — assume their inputs are sRGB by convention, and are converted automatically to the working color space. The remaining setters assume input is already in the working color space and perform no conversion, but this can be overridden with the `colorSpace` argument to any setter as shown on the THREE.Color documentation:

web.description:
However, colors passed to three.js shader must be Linear-sRGB.

- Add `colorSpace` argument to THREE.Color getters/setters
  - sRGB input will be converted to Linear-sRGB, as required by the renderer

- Many examples already use `renderer.outputEncoding=sRGB`, and so hard-coded colors (like background and ground colors) are implicitly Linear-sRGB... These will need to be updated (or their appearance will change) with color management enabled.

Color Management: Documentation\
#23430

|  |
|-|
| Update —- Color Management: Documentation #23430@Mugen87 to your question earlier, I believe that almost anything a user will 'do' with a Color instance should done in the working color space (Linear-sRGB, as defined in link above), and that's _not_ the color space users will find in a color picker or their CSS stylesheets, which are usually sRGB.If we define `color.encoding` or `color.colorSpace` and most colors get marked sRGB — since that is what users initialize them with! — there's very little you can safely do with the RGB components of that Color instance. Instead I think it's best to specify the color space of the input when constructing a color, and immediately convert to Linear-sRGB at that point. |

|  |
|-|
| > Vertex colors in glTF are linear multipliers...The glTF specification's phrasing of "linear multipliers" is something I'd prefer to leave out of three.js. It's clearer to say that both three.js vertex colors, `material.color`, `light.color`, etc. are expected to be given in Linear-sRGB space. The same is true of almost any role colors may fill in three.js. If we want to say that a loose/unused THREE.Color does not have a color space that's fine, but a Color used by a material or a light must be Linear-sRGB.> If a user is using a color picker, then the user needs to know something about color space conversion...The current state of three.js is that every time the user provides a color from virtually any other software, they must immediately do an explicit sRGB → Linear-sRGB conversion. The same is true for our own examples using `dat.gui` color pickers. It's good for users to know something about color space conversion, but requiring boilerplate conversion on every color input is not a good status quo, and not (IMO) standard practice in a graphics library. The objective of this PR is to ensure that a correct color workflow (with sRGB → Linear-sRGB conversion) is also the easiest color workflow. If this requires adding a stated assumption that certain THREE.Color instances contain RGB components in Linear-sRGB, I think we should do that. |

# Improve explanation on how to migrate from 151 to 152 color management#30305
## Material Properties
We assume sRGB and convert to Linear-sRGB only for hexadecimal and CSS-style color representations.

## Migration Steps
Otherwise, we render in Linear-sRGB, convert to sRGB, then blend and composite.

"Linear-sRGB color space" is kind of an oxymoron.

"Linear-sRGB color space" is kind of an oxymoron.

There are any number of possible linear color spaces, so I'm using the term "Linear-sRGB" as a shorthand for the particular color space with linear transfer functions, Rec. 709 "sRGB" primaries, and D65 white point.

This configuration is commonly known in the industry as "linear-sRGB."
